Surah 29: Al-'Ankabut (The Spider)

(Meccan, and it has sixty-nine verses)

﴿Alif. Lam. Mim.﴾ The discussion of this is like that which has passed repeatedly regarding its counterparts among the noble opening letters (al-fawatih al-karimah), except that what follows it cannot bear being connected to it by way of grammatical dependency (ta'alluq i'rabi, i.e., syntactic relation in i'rab, the grammatical inflection of words).

**Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on Surah 29, verse 2:**

﴿Do people think﴾ *al-ḥusbān* (supposing, reckoning) and its equivalents are not tied to the meanings of the individual words, but to the content of the sentences that establish something for something, or negate something of something, such that its two objects (*maf'ūlān*, the two direct objects of the verb) are derived from them. This is either by the verb itself, as in most cases, or by a type of alteration within them, as in the sentences introduced by *an* (that) and functioning as the relative clause (*ṣila*) of a relative pronoun, whether nominal or particle. Each of these is suitable for deriving its two objects from it, because the words of God Most High, ﴿Do people think that they will be left alone to say, "We believe," and that they will not be tested?﴾, are equivalent in meaning to *an*: it may be said, "Do they suppose themselves left alone without a trial merely by saying, 'We believe'?" Or it may be said, "Do they suppose that their being left untested after saying, 'We believe,' is an established reality?" The meaning is a denial of the aforementioned supposition and a declaration of it as unlikely, and an affirmation that God tests them with the hardships of the obligations, such as emigration (*muhājara*) and striving (*mujāhada*), abandoning what the soul desires, the duties of acts of obedience, and various kinds of calamities in their persons and possessions, so that the sincere is distinguished from the hypocrite, and the firm in religion from the wavering in it. And He recompenses them according to the ranks of their deeds, for mere faith, even if it is sincere, requires nothing beyond deliverance from abiding forever in the Fire.

It is narrated that it was revealed concerning some people among the Companions (*ṣaḥāba*), may God be pleased with them all, who became distressed by the harm inflicted by the polytheists. It was also said: it was revealed concerning 'Ammar, who was tortured for God's sake. And it was said: it was revealed concerning Mahja', the freed slave of 'Umar ibn al-Khaṭṭāb, may God be pleased with them both, whom 'Amir ibn al-Ḥaḍramī struck with an arrow on the day of Badr, killing him. His parents and his wife grieved over him, and he was the first of the Muslims to be martyred that day. The Messenger of God (ﷺ) said: "The master of the martyrs is Mahja', and he is the first of this community to be called to the gate of Paradise."

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 29, verse 3:

﴿And We certainly tested those before them﴾ is connected to His saying, ﴿Do people think...﴾ (the preceding verse, "aḥasiba"), or to His saying, ﴿they will not be tested﴾ (the preceding verse, "lā yuftanūn"). The meaning is that this is an ancient practice (sunnah qadīmah), founded upon far-reaching wisdoms (al-ḥikam al-bālighah), operating among all nations, so one should not expect its reversal. The meaning is also that the earlier nations suffered forms of trials (fitan) and afflictions (miḥan) more severe than what befell these people, and they endured, as His saying indicates: ﴿And how many a prophet fought, along with him many devoted followers; and they did not weaken for what befell them in the way of Allah, nor did they grow feeble, nor did they submit﴾ ... and the verses [that follow]. And from the Prophet (ﷺ): "Those before you would have a saw placed upon his head and be split into two halves, and that would not turn him from his religion; and he would be combed with iron combs, [tearing away] what lies beneath his bone of flesh and sinew, and that would not turn him from his religion."

﴿So Allah will certainly make known those who are truthful﴾, i.e., in their saying "We have believed."

﴿And He will certainly make known the liars﴾ in that. The "fa" (fa, "so") indicates that what follows is a consequence of what is revealed by what precedes it, namely the occurrence of the testing; and the "lam" (lam, the emphatic "la") is the answer to the oath. The turn to the Divine Name (al-ism al-jalīl) is to instill awe and to cultivate reverence, and the repetition of the answer is for added emphasis and affirmation. That is: by Allah, His knowledge will become attached to the testing in a manner that is actualized (taʿalluqan ḥāliyyan), by which those who were truthful in the faith they displayed are distinguished, and those who are liars in it, persisting in lying, are distinguished, and their recompenses of reward and punishment are consequently established. For this reason it has been said: the meaning is "He will distinguish," or "He will requite." It was also read: (وَلَيُعْلِمَنَّ) from the causative (min al-iʿlām), i.e., and He will make them known to people, or He will mark them with a sign by which they will be recognized on the Day of Resurrection, such as the whiteness and blackness of faces.

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 29, verse 4:

﴿Or do those who commit evil deeds think that they will outpace Us?﴾ That is: they will escape us, so that we would not be able to requite them for the evils of their deeds. This (clause) takes the place of the two objects of "ḥasiba" (to think/suppose), since it contains a predicate and a subject. "Am" (or) is disjunctive (munqaṭi'ah), and what it carries of the meaning of "bal" (rather) is for turning away (iḍrāb) and shifting (intiqāl) from rebuke by denying their supposing that they would be left unrequited and unpunished, to rebuke by denying something that is even more false than the first supposition, namely their supposing that they will not be requited for their evil deeds. Although they did not suppose that they could escape Him, the Exalted, and did not even entertain that notion in their souls, yet, since they persisted in sins and did not reflect on the outcome, they came to be in the position of one who hopes for that, as in His, the Exalted's, saying: ﴿He thinks that his wealth will make him immortal﴾.

﴿Evil is what they judge﴾. That is: wretched is the judgment they are passing; that judgment of theirs is wretched. Or: wretched is a judgment they pass, namely their judgment that.

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 29, verse 5:

﴿Whoever hopes for the meeting with Allah﴾ That is: he expects to encounter the recompense of Allah, whether reward or punishment, or the encounter with His judgment on the Day of Resurrection. It has also been said: "He hopes for the meeting with Allah, Mighty and Majestic, in Paradise." It has been said: "He hopes for His reward." It has been said: "He fears His punishment." It has also been said: the meeting with Him, exalted is He, is an expression for arriving at the final outcome, from the receiving of the Angel of Death, the resurrection, the reckoning, and the recompense, the situation being depicted by the situation of a servant who comes before his master after a long absence. His Master knows all that he used to do and neglect, so He will either meet him with cheerfulness and honor for what He was pleased with from his actions, or with the opposite for what He was angered by.

﴿Then indeed the term of Allah﴾ The ajal (term) is an expression for the end point of an extended span of time designated for some matter, and it may also be applied to that whole span of time; the first meaning is the more common in usage. That is: the time which Allah, exalted is He, has appointed for that ﴿is surely coming﴾ without doubt, with no diverting factor to turn it aside and no hindrance to restrain it; because the parts of time are constantly passing and elapsing, so that recompense too must surely come without fail, and the coming of its time necessarily entails the coming of the meeting. The answer (jawab) is omitted, meaning: let him choose from among the deeds that which leads to a good reward, and let him beware of what drives him to evil punishment, as in His saying, exalted is He: ﴿So whoever hopes for the meeting with his Lord, let him do righteous deeds and not associate anyone in the worship of his Lord﴾ [18:110], and in it is of promise and warning what is not hidden. It has also been said: let him hasten to that which fulfills his hope and confirms his expectation, or that which brings nearness and closeness (to Allah).

﴿And He is the All-Hearing﴾ of the words of the servants.

﴿the All-Knowing﴾ of their states, from the outward deeds and the beliefs.

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 29, verse 6:

﴿And whoever strives﴾ in obedience to Allah, Mighty and Majestic, ﴿then he strives only for himself﴾, because the benefit of it returns to him (p-31).

﴿Indeed, Allah is Free of need from the worlds﴾. So He has no need of their obedience, and He only commanded them to it to expose them to reward by the requirement of His mercy.

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 29, verse 7:

﴿And those who believe and do righteous deeds – We will surely remove from them their evil deeds﴾: that is, disbelief through faith, and sins through the acts of obedience that follow them.

﴿And We will surely reward them with the best of what they used to do﴾: that is, the best reward for their deeds, not merely the reward for the best of their deeds.

﴿And We enjoined upon man goodness toward his parents﴾. That is: by giving his parents and treating them with an action that is good, or with something that is itself good because of its great goodness, as in His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿And speak to people good words﴾. "وَصّى" (waṣṣā, "enjoined") functions as an imperative in meaning and usage, except that it is used for what the one commanded is to do that benefits either the one commanded or someone else. It was also said that it means "قال" (qāla, "said"), so the meaning would be: "And We said: Be good to your parents with goodness." It was also said that حُسْنًا (ḥusnan, "goodness") is in the accusative by an implied verb, as an explanatory statement of the enjoining, meaning: "And We said: Be kind to them," or "Do good to them." This is more fitting with what follows, and on this view it is good to stop at بِوالِدَيْهِ (biwālidayhi, "toward his parents"). It has been read as (ḥusnan) and (iḥsānan).

﴿And if they strive with you to make you associate with Me that of which you have no knowledge﴾. That is: regarding His divinity. He expressed its negation by the negation of knowledge of it, to indicate that what is not known to be true is not permissible to follow, even if its falsehood is not known. So how about what is known to be false?

﴿Then do not obey them﴾ in that, for there is no obedience to a creature in disobedience to the Creator. The implied speech must be supplied if it was not implied before. The prohibition of obeying them being linked to striving with them in the obligations indicates that the reason for the prohibition applies in what is less than that among the obligations, by way of greater priority.

﴿To Me is your return﴾. That is: the return of those of you who believed, and those who associated partners, and those who were good to their parents, and those who were undutiful.

﴿Then I will inform you of what you used to do﴾, by recompensing each of you for his deed: if good, then good, and if evil, then evil. The verse was revealed concerning Sa'd ibn Abi Waqqas, may Allah be pleased with him, at the time of his Islam, when his mother Hamnah bint Abi Sufyan ibn Umayyah swore that she would not move from the sun into the shade, nor eat, nor drink, until he reverted. She remained three days in this state. The same applies to the verse in Surat Luqman and Surat al-Ahqaf. It was also said that it was revealed concerning Ayyash ibn Abi Rabi'ah al-Makhzumi, that he emigrated with Umar ibn al-Khattab, may Allah be pleased with him, until they both reached Madinah. Abu Jahl and his brother from his mother, al-Harith ibn Asma', set out and came to Ayyash and said to him: "Indeed, among the religion of Muhammad (ﷺ) is maintaining ties of kinship and being good to parents. You have left your mother not eating, not drinking, and not sheltering under a roof until she sees you. So come out with us." And they induced him with a twisted cord at the top and the back [of the camel]. He consulted Umar, may Allah be pleased with him, who said: "They are deceiving you. And upon me is that I will divide my wealth between myself and you." But they kept at him until he obeyed them, and he disobeyed Umar, may Allah be pleased with him. Umar, may Allah be pleased with him, said: "As for you, since you have disobeyed me, take my she-camel, for there is no camel in this world that can catch up with her. If you have any doubt about them, then return." When they reached the desert, Abu Jahl said: "Indeed my she-camel has become exhausted, so take me up with you." So he dismounted to make room for himself behind him, and they seized him, bound him, and each of them lashed him a hundred lashes, and they brought him to his mother. She said: "You will remain in torment until you return from the religion of Muhammad."

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 29, verse 9:

﴿And those who believe and do righteous deeds – We will surely admit them among the righteous.﴾ That is: into the company of those firmly established in righteousness. Perfection in righteousness is the ultimate of the ranks of the believers and the utmost goal hoped for by the prophets and messengers of Allah. Allah the Exalted said, relating about Sulayman (peace be upon him): ﴿And admit me, by Your mercy, among Your righteous servants.﴾ And of Ibrahim (peace be upon him) He said: ﴿And indeed, he is in the Hereafter among the righteous.﴾ Or it means: in the place of entry of the righteous, which is Paradise.

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 29, verse 10:

﴿And among the people is he who says, "We believe in Allah," but when he is harmed for the sake of Allah﴾ i.e., regarding His cause, by the disbelievers torturing them for their faith, ﴿he regards the trial of people﴾ i.e., what befalls him of their harm, ﴿as the punishment of Allah.﴾

In severity and terror, so that he apostatizes from the religion, even though it has no measure at all compared with a single breath of His punishment, exalted is He.

﴿And if there comes a victory from your Lord﴾ i.e., a conquest and spoils,

﴿they will surely say﴾ with a damma on the lam, considering the meaning of "man" (man), just as the singular in what preceded is considering its wording. It has also been read with a fatha.

﴿"Indeed, we were with you"﴾ i.e., supporters of you in the religion, so give us a share of the booty. They were some of the weak Muslims who, whenever they were touched by harm from the disbelievers, would agree with them, and would conceal this from the Muslims. So Allah rebuked them with His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Is not Allah most knowing of what is in the breasts of the worlds?﴾ i.e., more knowing than they are of what is in their breasts of sincerity and hypocrisy, so that they do what they do of apostasy, concealment from the Muslims, and claiming to be of them in order to obtain the spoils. This is the most fitting for what preceded and what follows of His saying, exalted is He:

And Allah will surely know those who believe, that is, with sincerity.

And He will surely know the hypocrites (al-munafiqin), whether their disbelief was by harming the disbelievers or not. That is, He will surely recompense them for what they have of faith and hypocrisy (nifaq).

**"And those who disbelieve say to those who believe"** This explains how they drove the believers toward disbelief through enticement, after the previous explanation of how they drove them toward it through harm and threats. Here they are described as disbelievers, rather than in the way mentioned earlier, because the context of the discourse is to explain their crimes, whereas in what preceded it was to explain the crime of those whom they led astray. The **lam** (*lam al-tabligh*, the lam of conveying speech) indicates communication, meaning: they said, addressing them.

**"Follow our way"**: that is, take the path that we tread in religion. He expressed this with *ittiba'* (following), which is literally walking behind another walker, treating the path as if it were the one who travels it. Or the meaning is: follow us in our manner.

**"And let us bear your sins"**: that is, if that is a sin for which you will be held accountable by resurrection, as you say. They commanded themselves to bear the burden, placing it as a conjunction after their command to follow, to emphasise the connection of bearing the burden with following, and the promise of lightening their burdens if there were any burden. This was refuted by His saying, exalted is He: **"But they will not bear anything of their sins."** It was also read (*qur'a*, recited in a variant reading): "of their sins" (*min khati'atihim*). That is: they will not bear any part of their sins, which they had undertaken to bear in full. The first **min** is partitive (*lil-tabyin*, specifying), and the second is extra (*za'idah*, redundant), for totality (*lil-istighraq*, encompassing all). The clause is either a parenthetical interjection (*i'tiraD*) or a circumstantial clause (*hal*).

**"Indeed, they are liars"**: in that, in the course of their promise to bear the burden, they informed that they were capable of fulfilling what they promised. Lying, as it attaches to speech in terms of its explicit content, also attaches to it in terms of what its meaning necessarily entails, as was mentioned in His saying, exalted is He: **"Tell Me the names of these, if you are truthful."** (p-33)
