Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 29, verse 13:

﴿And they will surely bear their own burdens⁠﻿﻿﻿...⁠﻿⁠﻿ ...⁠﻿⁠﻿ ...⁠﻿⁠﻿ ...⁠﻿⁠﻿ ...⁠﻿⁠﻿ ...⁠﻿⁠﻿ ...⁠﻿⁠﻿...⁠﻿⁠﻿

I apologize, that attempt was garbled. Here is the clean translation:

﴿And they will surely bear their own burdens﴾: an explanation of what their saying that entails for them in the Hereafter of harm to themselves, after the explanation that it benefits those they address not at all. The expression of sins as "burdens" (athqal) is because of the extremity of their heaviness and their being crushing. The "lam" is the answer to an implied oath, meaning: by Allah, they will surely bear the full burdens of their own selves.

﴿And burdens﴾ others ﴿along with their burdens﴾: for what they caused through misguidance. Bearing [the burden of] disbelief and sins, without anything at all being diminished from the burdens of those whom they misled.

﴿And they will surely be questioned on the Day of Resurrection﴾ with a questioning of rebuke and reproach ﴿concerning what they used to fabricate﴾, meaning: what they invented in the world of falsehoods and fabrications, of which their present claim is part.

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 29, verse 14:

﴿And We certainly sent Noah to his people, and he remained among them a thousand years less fifty years﴾. This begins an account of the trials of the prophets, peace be upon them, from the harm inflicted by their nations, following the account of the trials of the believers from the harm of the disbelievers. This serves to emphasise the rebuke against those who think that they will be left merely for having faith, without being tested, and to urge them to patience. For the prophets, peace be upon them, when they were tested by what afflicted them from their nations of various kinds of hardships, and were patient under them, then it is all the more fitting and more deserving that these (believers) should be patient. It has been said: the lifespan of Noah, peace be upon him, was one thousand and fifty years; he was sent at the age of forty, and he called his people for nine hundred and fifty years, and he lived after the Flood for sixty years. And it is related from Wahb that he lived one thousand four hundred years. Perhaps the reason for the noble wording is to indicate the perfection of the number, for nine hundred and fifty may be used for what is close to it, and because mention of the thousand conveys an imagination of the length of the period. The purpose of the narrative is to console the Messenger of Allah ﷺ and to strengthen him in what he endured of suffering at the hands of the disbelievers, and to show the flimsiness of the opinion of those who think that they will be left without trial, and the variation of the distinguishing noun (thousand, then years) because repetition carries a kind of harshness.

﴿So the Flood seized them﴾. That is: immediately upon the completion of the stated period. "Al-Tufan" (the Flood) is applied to everything that encompasses a thing in abundance and intensity, of torrent, wind, or darkness, and it has become predominantly used for the flood of water.

﴿while they were wrongdoers﴾. That is: and the situation being that they were persistent in wrongdoing, they were not affected by what they heard from Noah, peace be upon him, of the signs, and they did not refrain from their disbelief and sins during this long period.

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 29, verse 15:

﴿So We delivered him﴾ i.e., Noah, peace be upon him.

﴿and the companions of the ship﴾ i.e., those who boarded it with him from among his children and followers. They were eighty in number. It was also said: seventy-eight; it was also said: ten; and it was said: eight, half of them males and half of them females.

﴿And We made it﴾ i.e., the ship, or the event and the story, ﴿a sign for the worlds﴾, by which they may take admonition.

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 29, verse 16:

﴿And Abraham﴾ is in the accusative by coordination with Noah (nuhan), and it was said: by supposing an implied "remember" (idhkur). It was also read in the nominative, on the assumption: "and among the messengers is Abraham." ﴿When he said to his people﴾: according to the first reading, it is an adverbial clause (zarf) governing the sending (al-irsal), i.e., "We sent him when his intellect had matured, he was able to reflect and to reason, and he advanced from the rank of perfection to the degree of completing others, since he took up the guidance of creation to the path of truth." According to the second reading, it is a substitution of inclusion (badal ishtimal) from Abraham.

﴿Worship Allah﴾, i.e., Him alone.

﴿And fear Him﴾, i.e., that you associate anything with Him.

﴿That is﴾, i.e., what has been mentioned of worship and god-fearing.

﴿Better for you﴾, i.e., than what you are upon. The sense of comparison (al-tafdil) is used although there is definitely no goodness in it, considering their false assumption.

﴿If you only knew﴾, i.e., good and evil, and could distinguish one from the other; or: if you know anything of things in any respect, for that is sufficient to judge that what he mentioned of worship and god-fearing is better.

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 29, verse 17:

﴿Indeed, you worship besides Allah only idols﴾ This is an explanation of the falsehood of their religion and of its evil in itself, after the explanation of its evil in relation to the true religion. That is: you worship besides Him, exalted is He, idols which are in themselves images fashioned by you, having no attribute other than that.

﴿And you invent a lie﴾ That is: and you lie a lie, in that you name them gods, and claim that they are your intercessors with Allah, exalted is He; or [it means] you make them and carve them for falsehood. It has been read (tukhalliqūna) with the doubling [of the lam], for intensification of the creating, in the sense of lying and fabricating; and (takhluqūna) with the dropping of one of the two tas from takhalluqa, in the sense of lying and fabricating falsely. It has also been read (ifkan), as a verbal noun like "al-kadhib" and "al-la'ib", or as an adjective in the sense of "khalqan dhā ifk" (a creation possessing falsehood).

﴿Indeed, those whom you worship besides Allah﴾ This is an explanation of the evil of what they worship, in that it hardly benefits them in any way.

﴿do not possess for you any provision﴾ That is: they are not able to provide you with anything of sustenance.

﴿So seek provision from Allah﴾ all of it, for He is the Provider, the Possessor of strength, the Firm.

﴿And worship Him﴾ alone, ﴿and be thankful to Him﴾ for His bounties, seeking your aims through worshipping Him, bound to thankfulness for what is already given, and seeking increase.

﴿To Him you will be returned﴾ That is: by death, then by resurrection, and to no other, so do what I have commanded you. It has been read (turja'ūna), from raja'a, rujū'an.

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 29, verse 18:

﴿And if you deny﴾, i.e., you deny me in what I have informed you of, that you will be returned to Him through resurrection (ba'th).

﴿then indeed nations before you denied﴾ is an explanation (ta'lil) for the answer, i.e., your denial will not harm me, for the nations before you denied the messengers before me, namely Shith, Idris, and Nuh, peace be upon them. Their denial did not harm them at all; rather it harmed only themselves, since it caused the punishment that befell them. So too is your denial.

﴿And upon the Messenger is only the clear conveyance﴾, i.e., the conveyance by which no doubt remains, and it is not incumbent upon him that his people believe him at all. He has indeed discharged the duty of conveyance with what admits of no addition, so your denial after that will not harm me at all.

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 29, verse 19:

﴿Have they not seen how Allah originates creation?﴾ This is a resumed statement (kalam mustanaf), directed from Him, Exalted is He, as a rebuke against their denial of the Resurrection despite the clarity of its proof and the openness of its path. The hamza (interrogative particle) is for denying their failure to see, which necessitates affirming it, and the waw is for conjunction with an implied element, i.e., "Have they not looked and not known, with a knowledge that runs parallel to sight in clarity and manifestness, the manner in which Allah, Exalted is He, originates creation, from a material and from no material?" That is, they have indeed known this. It has also been read with the second-person form (bi-sighat al-khitab) to intensify and emphasize the denial, and it has been read (yabda') [with a third-person verb]. His saying, Exalted is He, ﴿Then He will bring it back⦈ is a conjunction with "Have they not seen," not with "originates," because the seeing does not fall upon it. Thus it is an informing that He, Exalted is He, will bring creation back by analogy with the origination. It has also been permitted to conjoin it with "originates," by interpreting the return (i'adah) as His creating each year the like of what He created in the previous year of plants, fruits and other things. For that is among the things by which the soundness of the Resurrection and its occurrence without any doubt is established.

﴿Indeed that﴾ i.e., what has been mentioned of the return.

﴿is easy for Allah﴾ since He does not depend on anything at all.

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 29, verse 20:

﴿Say: Travel through the earth⦆ This is a command to Abraham, peace be upon him, that he should say this to them; that is, "Travel through it."

﴿and see how He originated creation⦆ That is, how He created them initially in various stages, with differing natures and diverse characters, for the arrangement of looking upon travel through the earth indicates the tracing of the conditions of the kinds of creatures who dwell in its regions.

﴿Then Allah brings about the final creation⦆ after the first creation that you have witnessed. The expression of the restoration, which is the point of dispute, as "the final creation," which implies that the beginning is a first creation, is for the purpose of alerting that the two are one matter among the matters of Allah, the Exalted, in reality and in name, insofar as each of them is an origination and a bringing forth from non-existence into existence, and there is no difference between them except in priority and posteriority. It was also read as (al-nashāʾah) with a long vowel, and both are dialects, like al-ra'fah and al-ra'āfah. Its place in the grammar is the accusative, as it is a emphatic infinitive (maṣdar) of "yunshi'" with the augmentations removed, the original being al-inshā'ah; or with the verb omitted, meaning: He brings into being, so they come into being in the final creation, as in His, the Exalted, saying: ﴿And He caused it to grow a goodly growth⦆. The sentence is conjoined to the sentence "Travel through the earth" and falls within the scope of the saying. The placing of the noble name, and its being made the subject while it is pronominalized in "badaʾa," serves to bring out greater care in explaining the realization of the restoration by pointing to the cause of the ruling, and the repetition of the predication. His, the Exalted, saying: ﴿Indeed Allah is over all things competent⦆ is a confirmation of what precedes by way of verification, for whoever knows the power of Allah, the Exalted, over all things, of which the restoration is one, cannot conceive of doubting His power over it, nor of its occurrence after He has informed of it.

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 29, verse 21:

﴿He punishes﴾: i.e., after the later creation (al-nash'a al-akhira).

﴿whom He wills﴾ to punish, and they are those who definitively deny it (the Hereafter).

﴿and has mercy on whom He wills﴾ to have mercy on, and they are those who affirm it. The clause completes what precedes it, and the placing of punishment first is because warning (al-tarhib) is more fitting to the context than encouragement (al-targhib).

﴿And to Him you will be returned﴾ at that time, not to other than Him, so that He does with you what He wills of punishment and mercy.

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 29, verse 22:

﴿And you cannot escape﴾ (i.e., you cannot frustrate) Him, the Exalted, in the implementation of His judgment and decree against you.

﴿on earth or in heaven﴾ That is, by hiding within the earth or by descending into its chasms, nor by seeking refuge in the heaven, which is more spacious than it, should you be able to ascend into it, as in His words, Exalted is He: ﴿If you are able to pass through the regions of the heavens and the earth, then pass through; you will not pass except with authority﴾ [55:33]; or by (fleeing to) the fortresses that rise up within it. It is also said that "in the heaven" is a qualifier of an omitted noun conjoined with "you" (antum), meaning: nor whoever is in the heaven.

﴿And you have not, besides Allah, any protector or any helper﴾ who would guard you from the affliction that befalls you, whether it emerges from the earth or descends from the heaven, and who would repel it from you.

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 29, verse 23:

﴿And those who disbelieve in the signs of Allah﴾ That is: in His proofs, both the created (takwiniyya) and the revealed (tanzīliyya), which indicate His essence, His attributes, and His acts. Thus the first creation (al-nash'a al-ūlā), which indicates the realization of resurrection (al-ba'th), enters into them at the primary level, as do the verses that speak of it. Restricting them to the proofs of His oneness (waḥdāniyya), exalted is He, is not suitable to the context.

﴿and His meeting﴾ which those signs speak of.

﴿Those﴾ are the ones described with what has been mentioned of disbelief in His signs, exalted is He, and in His meeting.

﴿They despair of My mercy﴾ That is: they will despair of it on the Day of Resurrection. The use of the past tense (ṣīghat al-māḍī) indicates its certainty; or they despair of it in this world, because of their denial of resurrection (al-ba'th) and recompense (al-jazā').

﴿And those — for them is a painful punishment﴾ The repetition of the demonstrative (ism al-ishāra), the repetition of the predication (al-isnād), the indefiniteness of "punishment" (al-'adhāb), and describing it as "painful" (al-alīm) all indicate, beyond doubt, the perfection of the atrociousness of their state. That is: those who are described by disbelief in the signs of Allah, exalted is He, and in His meeting, and by despair of His mercy, distinguished thereby from the rest of the disbelievers, for them, because of those ugly attributes, is a punishment whose measure cannot be estimated in severity and in causing pain.

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 29, verse 24:

﴿So what was the answer of his people﴾: it is read with the accusative (naṣb), on the basis that it is the predicate (khabar) of kāna and its subject (ism) is the saying of the Exalted: ﴿except that they said, "Kill him or burn him."﴾ It is also read with the nominative (raf'), in reverse. What is involved in this has already been discussed in its parallels. The intended meaning is not that nothing came from them in response to the proofs of Ibrahim, peace be upon him, except this monstrous statement, as is apparent from the outward wording of the noble verse. Rather, this was the answer on which they settled after the back-and-forth in the final instance. Otherwise, a countless number of superstitions and falsehoods issued from them. ﴿So Allah saved him from the fire.﴾ The fa' here is faṣīḥah (an connective particle indicating an unstated premise), meaning: so they threw him into the fire, and so Allah, the Exalted, saved him from it by making it, upon him be blessings and peace, cool and safe, as has been explained in other places. The manner of his being thrown into it and of Allah's saving him in detail has already been explained in Surat al-Anbiya'. It has been said: the fire did not benefit anyone on that day at all.

﴿Indeed, in that﴾: that is, in His saving him from it.

﴿are signs﴾: clear and wondrous signs, namely His preserving him from its heat, extinguishing it in a short time, and producing a garden in its place.

﴿for a people who believe.﴾ As for others, they are heedless of beholding them, and deprived of gaining the benefits of their traces.

﴿And [Abraham] said﴾, meaning Abraham, peace be upon him, addressing them: ﴿You have taken, besides Allah, idols only as a bond of affection between you in the life of this world﴾, meaning that you might show affection to one another and keep ties with one another through your gathering around their worship and your unity. The second object of *ittakhadhtum* (took) is omitted, meaning "idols as gods." It is permissible for *mawaddah* (affection) to be the object, either by supposing an omitted noun (the construct *mudaf*), or by interpreting it as "the beloved thing," or by taking it as the affection itself for emphasis, meaning: you have taken idols as a cause of affection between you, or as things beloved, or as affection itself. It was also read *mawaddatan* with tanwin in the accusative, functioning as the governor of the adverbial phrase (*zarf*) *baynakum* (between you). It was read in the nominative and in the construct form, as the predicate (*khabar*) of an omitted subject (*mubtada'*), meaning: "it is beloved," or "it is the affection itself," or "it is the cause of affection between you." The clause then serves as a qualifier (*sifah*) of *awthanan* (idols), or as the predicate of *inna* (indeed), if *ma* is a verbal-noun particle (*masdariyyah*) or a relative pronoun (*mawsulah*), in which case its returning pronoun, which is the first object, has been omitted. It was also read *mawaddatun* in the nominative with tanwin, and in the construct form with *bayni-kum* in the genitive, and *bayni-kum* was read with a fatha on the *bayn*, as in His saying ﴿Indeed your bond has been severed﴾ on one of the two readings. It was read *innama mawaddatu baynikum*, and the meaning is that your taking them as a bond of affection between you lasts only in this life. You have applied its rulings, since you did to me what you did out of love for them, defending them against me, as His saying indicates: ﴿And help your gods﴾.

﴿Then on the Day of Resurrection﴾ matters will be reversed, affection will turn into hatred, and gentle courtesy into mutual cursing, where ﴿some of you will disown others﴾, these being the worshippers, ﴿...some others﴾, these being the idols, ﴿and some of you will curse others﴾, meaning that each group among you and among the idols will curse the other group, since Allah will cause them to speak. ﴿And your refuge is the Fire﴾, meaning it is your abode to which you return, and you will never come out of it. ﴿And you will have no helpers﴾ who will rescue you from it, just as my Lord rescued me from the fire into which you cast me. The plural *nasirin* (helpers) is used because it is set against a plural, meaning that none of you has any helper at all.

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 29, verse 26:

﴿So Lut believed him.﴾ That is, he affirmed him in all of his statements, not merely in his prophethood; and [he affirmed] only what he called to of monotheism (tawhid), for he was free of disbelief. As for what was said, that he believed in him when he saw the fire not burning him, it should be interpreted in line with what we have mentioned, or it may be meant that faith here refers to its lofty rank, which only the aspirations of the perfected individuals can reach. Lut was the son of his brother, peace be upon them both.

﴿And he said: Indeed I am migrating﴾ That is, away from my people.

﴿to my Lord﴾ to wherever my Lord commands me. ﴿Indeed He is the Mighty﴾ the one who prevails over His affair, so He protects me from my enemies.

﴿the Wise﴾ the one who does not perform any act except that it contains wisdom and benefit, so He commands me only with what is good for me. It is narrated that he migrated from Kuthaa, in the outskirts of Kufa, together with Lut and Sarah, the daughter of his paternal uncle, to Harran, and then from there to the Levant (al-Sham), where he settled in Palestine, and Lut settled in Sodom.

The commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 29, verse 27:

﴿And We bestowed upon him Isaac and Jacob﴾: a son, and a grandson (nafilah), when he had despaired of a barren old woman.

﴿And We placed in his offspring prophethood﴾: so many of his descendants were prophets.

﴿And the Book﴾: i.e., the genus of Scripture (al-kitab), encompassing the four books.

﴿And We gave him his reward﴾ in return for his emigration (hijrah, migration) to Us ﴿in this world﴾: by granting him a son, righteous offspring, the continuation of prophethood among them, the adherence of the followers of the religious communities (milal) to him, and praise and blessings upon him until the end of time.

﴿And indeed he, in the Hereafter, is among the righteous﴾: i.e., those who are perfect in righteousness.

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 29, verse 28:

﴿Lot﴾ (Lut) is in the accusative case, either by conjunction with "Nuh" or with "Ibrahim." The discussion of His words, exalted is He, ﴿when he said to his people﴾ is like what has passed in the story of Ibrahim, peace be upon him.

﴿Indeed, you commit an abomination﴾, that is, the act that is extremely ugly. It has been read as (a-innakum) [with an interrogative hamza]. ﴿No one in the worlds has preceded you in it﴾ is a resumptive clause (isti'naf) confirming the perfection of its ugliness, for the consensus of all individuals of the worlds on avoiding it is only because it is something that human natures recoil from and souls shrink away from.

Abu al-Su'ud, Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim, on surah 29, verse 29:

(p-38) ﴿Do you indeed approach men and cut off the road﴾ and attack travellers (al-sabilah), meaning: the abomination, since it is related that they often committed it with strangers. It was also said: "they cut off the path of women by turning away from tilth (al-harth) and by going in to what is not tilth." It was also said: "they cut off the road by killing and seizing property."

﴿And commit in your assembly﴾, meaning: you do in your gathering (majlis) that brings together your companions.

﴿the evil deed﴾, such as intercourse, flatulence, untying the waistwrap, and other shameful acts of wrongdoing in which there is no good. It is reported from Ibn 'Abbas, may Allah be pleased with him, that it is throwing pebbles, shooting with pellet-bows (al-banadiq), snapping the fingers (al-farqa'ah), chewing gum (al-'ilk), using the siwak among people, untying the waistwrap, cursing (al-sibab), and obscene talk in jest. It was also said: mocking those who passed by them. It was also said: openly displaying that deed in their assembly.

﴿So the answer of his people was only that they said: "Bring us the punishment of Allah, if you are among the truthful"﴾, meaning: their answer was nothing at all from them except this shameful statement; that is, it did not come from them on this occasion, out of the occasions of Lot's admonitions, peace be upon him, in which he had threatened them with punishment. As for what is in Surah al-A'raf in the words of the Exalted: ﴿And the answer of his people was only that they said: "Expel them from your town"﴾ ... the verse, and what is in Surah al-Naml in the words of the Exalted: ﴿So the answer of his people was only that they said: "Expel the family of Lot from your town"﴾ ... the verse, that is what came from them after this occasion, and this is the last occasion of the exchanges that took place between them and him, peace be upon him. Its verification has already passed in Surah al-A'raf.

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 29, verse 30:

﴿He said: "My Lord, help me against the corrupting people."﴾ That is, by sending down the promised punishment.

﴿Against the corrupting people﴾: by innovating the vile deed, establishing it as a practice for those after them, persisting in it, and hastening the punishment by way of mockery. He described them with this only to emphasize the request for the punishment to descend upon them.

The Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 29, verse 31:

﴿And when Our messengers came to Ibrahim with the good news﴾, i.e., with the glad tidings of a son and a grandson (nafila). ﴿They said﴾, i.e., to Ibrahim, peace be upon him, within the course of the speech, as was detailed in Surat Hud and Surat al-Hijr.

﴿Indeed, we are going to destroy the people of this town﴾, i.e., the town of Sodom (Sadum). The construction here is a lafzi idafa (a grammatical genitive construction that is nominal in form only), because the meaning is future (al-istiqbal).

﴿Indeed, its people were wrongdoers﴾: this is a causal clause (ta'lil) giving the reason for the destruction, namely their persistence in wrongdoing, their excess in various kinds of corruption, and their types of sins.

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 29, verse 32:

﴿He said, "Indeed, Lut is there."﴾ So how could you destroy it? ﴿They said, "We know best who is in it. We will surely save him and his family."﴾ They meant that they were not unaware of the place of Lut, peace be upon him, within it; rather, they meant that they were not unaware of those who had not been targeted by Ibrahim, peace be upon him, among his believing followers. They were also taking the utmost care of their affair, as is indicated by the opening of the promise of deliverance with an oath, i.e., "By Allah, we will surely save him and his family."

﴿Except his wife; she was among those who remained behind.﴾ That is, those who remained behind in the punishment, or in the town.

(p-39) ﴿And when Our messengers came to Lot﴾ — those mentioned, after they had parted from Ibrahim, peace be upon him — ﴿he was distressed on their account﴾: distress overtook him because of them, fearing that his people would harm them. The word "an" (أنْ) here is an added particle (صِلَة) to emphasize the connection between the two verbs.

﴿And he was grieved for them⁠﴾ — that is, he was straitened in regard to their affair and the management of their matter; his ﴿dharʿ﴾ (ذَرْع) — i.e., his capacity — fell short, as in their saying "his hand was narrowed." Its opposite is "his dharʿ was broad concerning such-and-such," meaning he was able to cope with it and capable of it, for the long-armed reaches what the short-armed cannot reach.

﴿And they said﴾ — when they observed in him signs of impatience on their account, and saw that he was unable to repel his people after much effort, until the situation reached the point where he said: ﴿"Would that I had strength against you, or could take refuge in a mighty pillar!"⁠﴾

﴿"Fear not"⁠﴾ — that is, of your people regarding us.

﴿"Nor grieve"⁠﴾ — that is, over anything. It was also said: over our destroying them.

﴿"Indeed, we will save you and your family"⁠﴾ from what will befall them of the punishment.

﴿"Except your wife; she is of those who remain behind"⁠﴾. It is also read: (لَنُنَجِيَنَّكَ) and (مُنَجُّوكَ), from ﴿al-injaʾ﴾ (الإنجاء, "rescue"). In either case, the place of the kaf (ك) is in the genitive case according to the preferred view, and the accusative of ﴿ahlaka﴾ (أهلَكَ) is by an implied verb, or by coordination with its grammatical position in terms of the original form.

Verse 29:34: "Indeed We are sending down upon the people of this town a punishment (rijz) from the sky."

This is a resumptive sentence (isti'naf, a new clause that begins a fresh statement) brought to explain what was indicated by the promise of deliverance (wa'd al-tanjiyah): the descent of punishment upon them. Al-rijz (punishment) is the chastisement that disturbs the one who is punished, i.e., unsettles and agitates him. It is derived from their saying: irtajaza, when something shakes and is agitated (ertajasa wa-idtaraba). It is also read as (munazzilun) with the doubled zay (tashdid).

"For that they used to commit wickedness (fisq)": i.e., because of their persistent corruption and defiance.

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 29, verse 35:

﴿And We have certainly left of it﴾ i.e., of the town.

﴿a clear sign﴾ — that is, its wondrous story and the traces of its ruined dwellings. It has been said: the rain of stones, for it remained after them; and it has been said: the black water upon the surface of the earth.

﴿for a people who use reason﴾ — who employ their intellects in discernment and reflection (i'tibar). This phrase is related either to "We have left" or to "clear [sign]."

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 29, verse 36:

﴿And to Madyan [We sent] their brother Shu'ayb.﴾ It is connected to an implied verb coordinated with "We sent" in the story of Noah, peace be upon him; that is: "And We sent to Madyan Shu'ayb."

﴿So he said: O my people, worship Allah﴾ alone.

﴿And hope for the Last Day﴾ That is: expect it, and what will befall in it of kinds of terrors, and do today such deeds as will make you safe from its harm. It has also been said: "And hope for its reward," by way of putting the cause in place of the effect. It has also been said: "hope" here means "fear."

﴿And do not commit abomination in the land, causing corruption.﴾

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 29, verse 37:

﴿So they denied him, and the quake seized them.﴾ That is: the violent earthquake (al-zalzalah al-shadidah).

In Surat Hud, ﴿And those who did wrong were seized by the Cry (al-sayhah)﴾, that is: the Cry of Jibril, peace be upon him. For it is the Cry that necessitates the quake, through its causing the air to undulate and what lies adjacent to it of (p-40) the earth.

﴿Then they were in their abode by morning﴾: that is, in their land (baladihim), or their dwellings (manazilihim). The singular (dar) is used to avoid ambiguity (li-amn al-labs).

﴿Lying prostrate (jathimin)﴾: crouching on their knees, dead (mayyitin).

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 29, verse 38:

﴿And ʿAd and Thamud﴾: both are in the accusative, governed by a verb understood (ʾidmar) implied by what precedes them, i.e., "We destroyed." It has also been read as "Thamudā" (with tanwin), on the reinterpretation of the tribe as a group (al-hayy).

﴿And it has become clear to you from their dwellings﴾: i.e., it has become evident to you that We destroyed them, from their dwelling places, by looking at them when you pass by them on your journey to Syria and on your return from it.

﴿And Satan made their deeds appear fair to them﴾: from among the various kinds of disbelief and disobedience.

﴿So he barred them from the path﴾: the straight path that leads to the truth. ﴿And they were discerning﴾: able to reflect and to reason. Yet they did not do so. Or: they were clearly aware that punishment would befall them, through the warning of their messengers, peace be upon them, to them, but they persisted stubbornly until they met what they met.

Qarun, Pharaoh and Haman [are also mentioned]: ﴿وَقارُونَ وفِرْعَوْنَ وهامانَ﴾ is in apposition (conjoined) to "Ad". It was said: Qarun is mentioned first because of the nobility of his lineage.

﴿وَلَقَدْ جاءَهم مُوسى بِالبَيِّناتِ فاسْتَكْبَرُوا في الأرْضِ وما كانُوا سابِقِينَ﴾ meaning: escaping, eluding, from their saying: "سَبَقَ طالِبَهُ" (he outran his pursuer) when he escaped him and was not overtaken. And indeed the command of Allah, mighty and majestic, overtook them, with what an overtaking, so they were brought to ruin and destruction.

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 29, verse 40:

﴿So each one﴾ is an explanation of what is indicated by their not being mentioned in a general manner; that is, each one of those mentioned ﴿We seized for his sin﴾, that is, We punished him for his crime, not some of them and not others, as the fronting of the object (in the Arabic) indicates.

﴿Among them is one upon whom We sent a hasib (a violent storm of pebbles)﴾ is a detailed explanation of the seizing; that is, a fierce wind in which there were pebbles. It was also said: an angel who pelted them with stones, namely the people of Lut.

﴿And among them is one seized by the Cry﴾ such as Madyan and Thamud.

﴿And among them is one whom We caused the earth to swallow﴾ such as Qarun.

﴿And among them is one whom We drowned﴾ such as the people of Nuh, and Fir'awn and his people.

﴿And Allah would never wrong them﴾ by what He did to them, for that is impossible on His part, may He be exalted.

﴿But they were wronging themselves﴾ by persisting in committing what necessitates that, of the types of disbelief and disobedience.

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 29, verse 41:

﴿The likeness of those who take protectors other than Allah﴾ means: in what they have taken as a reliance and a support.

﴿Is like the spider, which takes a house﴾ in what it weaves, in weakness and frailty. Rather, that is weaker than this, because it has a reality and some benefit in general; or their likeness, in relation to the One God, is like the likeness of a man who built a house of stone and gypsum. The spider (al-'ankabut) applies to the singular and the plural, the masculine and the feminine, and the common usage is the feminine, and its ta' is like the ta' in taghut (the ta' of feminine form), and it is pluralized as 'anakib and 'ankabutat. As for al-'ikab, al-'ukub and al-a'kub, these are collective nouns (asma' al-jumu').

﴿And indeed, the weakest of houses is the house of the spider﴾ since nothing is seen that approaches it in weakness and fragility.

﴿If only they knew﴾ means: anything at all of things, they would have been certain that this is their likeness, or that their religion is, or it is among that. It is permissible that the house of the spider be made an expression for their religion, to realize the comparison; so the meaning is: and indeed the weakest of what is relied upon in religion is their religion.

**Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 29, verse 42:**

﴿Indeed, Allah knows what they call upon besides Him, of anything.﴾ This is according to the implied (*idmar*, the omission of a word understood from context) of a verb of saying, meaning: Say to the disbelievers, "Indeed Allah..." etc. The *ma* is interrogative (*istifhamiyya*), in the accusative case as the object of *yad'una* ("they call upon"), and it is suspended (*mu'allaqah*) the verb *ya'lamu* ("He knows") from acting on it. The *min* is either explicative (*lil-tabyin*) or negative, and the *min* is additional (*mazida*, grammatically superfluous), and *shay'in* ("anything") is the object of *yad'una*. Or the *ma* is verbal-noun (*masdariyya*), and *shay'in* refers to the verbal noun. Or the *ma* is relative (*mawsula*), the object of *ya'lamu*, and the object of *yad'una* is its omitted returning pronoun. It is also read *tad'una* with a *ta'*, and the statement according to the first two readings is a rebuke of them (*tajhil*) and an emphasis of the parable; according to the last two it is a warning (*wa'id*) to them.

﴿And He is the Mighty, the Wise.﴾ This is a reason (*ta'lil*) for both meanings. The association of that which is not counted as anything with One who is of such a status is a result of extreme foolishness. Moreover, an inanimate object, in relation to the Capable, the Subduer over everything, who has reached the utmost in knowledge and in perfection of action, is like pure non-existence. And the One who has these attributes is capable of recompensing them.

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 29, verse 43:

﴿And these parables – We strike them for the people﴾: that is, this parable and its like.

﴿To bring near what is far from their understanding.﴾

﴿But none understands them﴾ as they truly are in their beauty and in the benefits that follow from them, ﴿except those of knowledge﴾: the rooted in knowledge (al-rasikhun fi al-'ilm), those who reflect upon things as they should be reflected upon. And from him (ﷺ), that he recited this verse and said: "The learned person is one who understands from Allah the Exalted, acts in obedience to Him, and avoids His displeasure."

That is: [creating them] in truth, while observing the wisdoms and benefits, this being a circumstantial qualifier (ḥāl) of the subject of khalaqa (the one who created). Or [it means] they are connected with the truth from which there is no turning away, bringing in its wake religious and worldly benefits, this being a circumstantial qualifier of its object. For they, together with containing everything on which their livelihoods depend, are evidences indicating the Exalted One's matters connected with His essence and attributes, as His words, exalted is He, make clear: ﴿Indeed, in that is a sign for the believers﴾, indicating to them what has been mentioned of His matters, glory be to Him. The specification of the believers by mention, despite the generality of guidance and direction in their creation for everyone, is because they are the ones who benefit from that.

﴿Recite what has been revealed to you of the Book﴾ — drawing near to God Most High through its recitation, reflecting on the meanings within it, reminding the people, and urging them to act upon its rulings, its noble etiquettes, and its excellent moral virtues.

﴿And establish the prayer﴾ — that is, persist in establishing it. Since the prayer encompasses the obligatory prayers performed in congregation, and his (ﷺ) command to establish it implied a command to the community to do so, it is explained by God's words: ﴿Indeed, the prayer forbids indecency and wrongdoing﴾. It is as if it were said: "Lead them in prayer, for the prayer forbids them from indecency and wrongdoing." The meaning of "its forbidding them from these two" is that it is a cause of refraining from them, because it is a private conversation with God Most High, so it must be accompanied by complete attentiveness to obeying Him and total turning away from His disobedience. Ibn Mas'ud and Ibn 'Abbas, may God be pleased with them both, said: "In the prayer there is a point of cessation and a deterrent from the disobedience of God Most High. Whoever his prayer does not command him to good, and does not restrain him from wrongdoing, his prayer only increases him in distance from God Most High." Al-Hasan and Qatadah said: "Whoever his prayer does not restrain from indecency and wrongdoing, his prayer is a burden upon him." Anas, may God be pleased with him, related: "A young man from the Ansar used to pray with the Messenger of God (ﷺ), yet he would not leave any of the indecencies without committing it. The Messenger of God (ﷺ) was told of his condition, and he said: 'Indeed, his prayer will restrain him.' He did not remain long before he repented and his condition became good."

﴿And the remembrance of God is greater﴾ — that is, the prayer is greater than the rest of the acts of obedience. He expressed it by this (i.e., by the remembrance of God), as in His words: ﴿So hasten to the remembrance of God﴾, to indicate that the remembrance of God Most High contained within it is the principal element that makes it superior to the good deeds and a restraint from the evil deeds. It has also been said: "The remembrance of God Most High at the time of indecency and wrongdoing, and the mention of His prohibition of them and His warning against them, is greater in deterring from them." It has also been said: "The remembrance of God Most High of you with His mercy is greater than your remembrance of Him with your obedience."

﴿And God knows what you do﴾ — of it, and of the rest of the acts of obedience, so He will reward you for them in the best of recompense.

**Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 29, verse 46:**

﴿And do not argue with the People of the Book﴾ — from the Jews and the Christians — ﴿except in the best manner﴾; that is, with the manner that is best, such as meeting harshness with gentleness, anger with restraint, contentiousness with sincere advice, and hostility with patience, in a way that does not indicate weakness and does not lead to yielding what is base. It has been said: it is abrogated by the verse of the sword.

﴿except those of them who have wronged﴾ by excessive aggression and obstinacy, or by ascribing a son [to God], and their saying: ﴿The Hand of God is chained﴾ and the like. For in that case it is obligatory to repel them by what befits their condition.

﴿And say: We believe in what has been sent down to us﴾ of the Qur'an, ﴿and what has been sent down to you﴾; that is, and in what has been sent down to you of the Torah and the Gospel. The manner of believing in both has already been verified at the end of Surah al-Baqarah. And from the Prophet (ﷺ): "Do not believe the People of the Book, nor disbelieve them, but say: We believe in God, His books, and His messengers. If they say something false, do not affirm it; and if they say something true, do not deny it." ﴿And our God and your God is One﴾, having no partner in divinity.

﴿And we are to Him submitting﴾ — obedient exclusively. In this there is an allusion to the condition of both groups, in that they took their rabbis and their monks as lords besides God.

(Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud, Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim, on surah 29, verse 47)

﴿And thus﴾ is a turning of the address to the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ). "Thus" (dhalika) is a reference to the verbal noun (masdar) of the verb that follows it, and the sense of distance contained in it (dhalika) serves to indicate the great distinction of the one referred to in excellence; that is: "Like that wondrous sending down, which is in harmony with the sending down of all the other Books, ﴿We have sent down to you the Book﴾," i.e., the Qur'an, of which this verse, which speaks of disputing in the best manner as mentioned, is part.

﴿Those to whom We have given the Book﴾ from among the two groups ﴿believe in it﴾. By them is meant Abdullah ibn Salam and his like from among the People of the Book specifically, as if those others among them had not been given the Book, since they did not act upon what is in it. Or it refers to those among them who preceded the time of the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ), since they were affirming its descent as they witnessed in their two Books. Singling them out for being given the Book serves to indicate that those after them among the contemporaries of the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) had the Book removed from them by abrogation (naskh), so they were not given it. The "fa'" (so/then) is for the sequencing of what follows upon what precedes, for their belief in it is consequent upon its being sent down in the manner mentioned.

﴿And among these﴾, i.e., and among the Arabs, or the people of Makkah according to the first interpretation, or those of his time (ﷺ) according to the second,

﴿are those who believe in it﴾, i.e., in the Qur'an.

﴿And none deny Our signs﴾: He expressed the Book by "signs" (ayat) to draw attention to the clear manifestation of its indications of its meanings and to its being from Allah the Exalted. It is ascribed to the plural of majesty ("We") for greater magnification of it and the utmost reproach of whoever denies it.

﴿except the disbelievers﴾, those who plunge deeply into disbelief and are determined upon it, for that prevents them from reflecting on what would lead them to recognizing its truth. It has been said that they are Ka'b ibn al-Ashraf and his companions.

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 29, verse 48:

﴿And you did not recite any scripture before it﴾, i.e., before Our sending the Book down to you, you were not able to recite anything from any scripture.

﴿Nor did you write it with your right hand﴾, i.e., you were not able to write it.

﴿With your right hand﴾: as is customary, or it was not your habit to recite it or to write it.

﴿Otherwise, the falsifiers would have had doubts﴾, i.e., had you been one who is able to recite and write, or one who habitually did so, they would have doubted and said: "Perhaps he gathered it from the books of the ancients." Since you were not like that, there remains no basis at all for doubt concerning your affair. Calling them "falsifiers" (mubtiluna) in their doubting, on the supposed premise, is because they are falsifiers in following this possibility, despite the manifest purity of the Prophet (ﷺ) from such things.

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 29, verse 49:

﴿Nay, it﴾ i.e., the Qur'an.

﴿is clear signs﴾, evident, firmly established, ﴿in the breasts of those who have been given knowledge﴾, without being taken from a book that they memorize in such a way that no one can alter it. ﴿And none deny Our signs﴾, while they are as has been mentioned.

﴿except the wrongdoers﴾, those who exceed the limits in evil, obstinacy, and corruption.

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 29, verse 50:

﴿And they say: "Why were no signs sent down upon him from his Lord?"﴾ Like the she-camel of Salih, the staff of Musa, and the table of Isa, upon them be peace. It is also read as "āyah" (a single sign). ﴿Say: "Signs are only with Allah"﴾ He sends them down as He wills, without anyone having any say in that whatsoever.

﴿And I am only a clear warner﴾ It is not my task except to warn with what I have been given of the signs.

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 29, verse 51:

﴿Is it not sufficient for them﴾ This is a resumed statement (kalam mustani'af) coming from Him, exalted is He, as a rebuttal of their demand (iqtirah) and as a clarification of its invalidity. The hamzah (interrogative particle) here is for denial and negation, and the waw is for conjunction (ʿatf) upon an implied element that the context requires, meaning: "Have they fallen short, and has it not sufficed them that there is a sign which suffices in place of all other signs?"

﴿That We have sent down to you the Book﴾ the one that speaks the truth, confirming what lies before it of the heavenly scriptures, while you were far removed from studying (mudarasah) them and practising (mumarasah) them.

﴿being recited to them﴾ in every time and place, so there is always with them an enduring sign that does not vanish or perish, unlike every other sign which passes away after its occurrence and exists in one place but not another. Or it means: it is recited to the Jews, by confirming what is in their hands concerning your description and the description of your religion.

﴿Surely in that﴾ the Great Book, (p-44) whose matter remains through the passing of ages,

﴿is a mercy﴾ meaning: a great blessing.

﴿and a reminder﴾ meaning: an admonition.

﴿for a people who believe﴾ meaning: for a people whose concern is faith, not obstinate fault-finding (ta'annut) like those who made these demands. It is said that some of the believers came to the Messenger of God (ﷺ) with a shoulder-blade (katif) in which was some of what the Jews were saying. He said: "It is enough error for a people that they turn away from what their prophet brought to what was brought by someone other than their prophet." Then this was revealed.

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 29, verse 52:

﴿Say: "Allah suffices as a witness between me and you."﴾ (regarding) what has proceeded from me and from you.

﴿He knows whatever is in the heavens and the earth.﴾ That is: of the matters of which my affair and your affair are part. It is therefore a confirmation of what came before it, namely His sufficiency as a witness.

﴿And those who believe in falsehood﴾ — and this is what is worshipped besides Allah, the Exalted.

﴿and disbelieve in Allah﴾ — despite the convergence of the factors that necessitate belief in Him.

﴿It is those who are the losers﴾ — those who are defrauded in their transaction, in that they exchanged faith for disbelief, by losing the original innate disposition (fitrah) and the transmitted evidences (al-adillah al-sam'iyyah) that necessitate belief. The verse is of the type of "arguing in the best manner" (al-mujadalah bi-allati hiya ahsan), since it does not explicitly attribute the belief in falsehood, the disbelief in Allah, and the loss to them, but rather mentions them in the manner of ambiguity (al-ibham), as in His Exalted saying: ﴿And indeed, we or you are surely upon guidance or in clear error.﴾

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 29, verse 53:

﴿And they ask you to hasten the punishment﴾, in the manner of mockery, by their saying: ﴿When is this promise?﴾ and their saying: ﴿So rain down upon us stones from the sky, or bring us a painful punishment﴾, and the like of that.

﴿Had it not been for a term appointed﴾, which Allah, exalted is He, had set for their punishment and specified in the Preserved Tablet (al-Lawh).

﴿the punishment would have come upon them﴾, the one specified for them, in accordance with what they asked to hasten. It has been said: the intended term is the Day of Resurrection, based on what is related, that Allah, exalted is He, promised the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) that He would not punish his people with a punishment that uproots them, and that He would delay their punishment until the Day of Resurrection. It has also been said: it is the Day of Badr. And it has been said: it is the time of their perishing at their appointed terms. But this view is clearly remote, since they were not promised their natural death, nor were they seeking to hasten it.

﴿And it will surely come upon them﴾ is a resumed sentence explaining what was alluded to in the preceding sentence concerning the coming of the punishment at the arrival of the appointed term; that is: by Allah, the punishment specified for them will surely come upon them at the arrival of the term.

﴿suddenly﴾, that is: unexpectedly.

﴿while they do not perceive﴾, that is: its coming. Perhaps the intended meaning of its coming in this way is that it will not come upon them through hastening it in response to their urging and granting their request, for that would be a coming in accordance with their wish and awareness. Rather, it will come upon them while they are heedless, secure, not bringing it to mind, like the custom of some punishments descending upon some nations by night while they sleep, or in the forenoon while they play, because the coming of the punishment of the Hereafter and the punishment of the Day of Badr is not of this kind.

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 29, verse 54:

﴿They ask you to hasten the punishment, and indeed Hell encompasses the disbelievers.﴾ This is a resumptive (isti'naf) clause, brought to show the extent of their ignorance and the feebleness of their opinion. It also indicates that what they asked to hasten is the punishment of the Hereafter, i.e., "they ask you to hasten the punishment." The situation is that the place of the punishment, which is a punishment above which there is none, encompasses them, as if it were said: "They ask you to hasten the punishment, and indeed the punishment encompasses them," i.e., it will encompass them. The nominal sentence (al-jumla al-ismiyya) is used to indicate the certainty of the encompassing and its continuity, or by way of treating the state of the cause as the state of the effect. For disbelief and the sins that necessitate entry into Hell encompass them. It is also said: disbelief and sins are in reality the Fire, but they have appeared in this world in this form. Its detailed explanation has passed in surah al-A'raf at His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And the weighing on that day is the truth﴾. The "al-" in "al-kafirin" is either for specific reference (al-'ahd), with the placing of the apparent noun in the place of the pronoun to indicate the cause of the ruling, or for the generic (al-jins), and they are included in it by primary inclusion.

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 29, verse 55:

﴿The Day the punishment will envelop them﴾ is an adverbial complement (zarf) governing an implied verb whose mention has been omitted, to signal the utmost extent of its magnitude and terror. It is as if it were said: "On the Day the punishment will envelop them—the punishment indicated by the encompassing of them by Hell—there will be states and terrors such that speech cannot express them." It has also been said that it is an adverbial complement of "encompassing" (al-ihatah).

﴿From above them and from beneath their feet﴾: that is, from all their directions.

﴿And He will say﴾: that is, Allah, Mighty and Majestic. This is supported by the reading with the plural of majesty (nun al-'azamah), or it is some of His angels by His command.

﴿Taste what you used to do﴾: that is, the recompense for what you used to do in the world, continuously, of evil deeds, among which is seeking hasty punishment.

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 29, verse 56:

﴿O My servants who believe﴾: an address of honour to those believers who are unable to establish the affairs of the religion as they should because of obstruction from the disbelievers, and a guidance for them to the safer path.

﴿Indeed, My earth is vast, so worship Me alone﴾: that is, if worship cannot be easily performed in one land and you cannot manifest your religion, then emigrate to wherever that becomes possible for you. And from him (ﷺ): "Whoever flees with his religion from one land to another, even if it is a span of land, has earned Paradise and will be the companion of Ibrahim and Muhammad, peace be upon them both."

The "fa" (فَ) is the response (jawab) of an elided conditional clause (shart mahdhuf), since the meaning is: "Indeed My earth is vast; if you do not sincerely worship Me in one land, then sincerely worship Me in another." Then the conditional clause was elided, and in its place the object was fronted (taqdim al-maf'ul), which conveys the meaning of exclusivity (ikhtisas) and sincerity (ikhlas).

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 29, verse 57:

﴿Every soul shall taste death; then to Us you will be returned.﴾ This is an independent (resumptive) sentence, brought in to urge hastening to comply with the command. That is: every soul among souls experiences the bitterness of death and its anguish, and then returns to Our judgment and Our recompense, according to its deeds. For whoever has this as his end, there is no escape from taking provision for it and preparing for it. And it has been read (as): (yurja'un) [with the verb in the passive voice, "you will be returned" becoming "they will be returned"].

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 29, verse 58:

﴿And those who believe and do righteous deeds – We will surely settle them⁠﴾ meaning: We will surely cause them to descend.

﴿in the lofty chambers of Paradise⁠﴾ i.e., upper stories (ʿalālī). It is the second object of al-tabwiʾah (settling), and it is recited as (lanuthawwiyannahum) from al-thawāʾ, meaning residence. The accusative of "ghurafan" is then either by treating it as if it were in the sense of "lanunazzilannahum" (We will surely cause them to descend), or by removing the preposition, or by likening the time-specified adverb to the indefinite, as in His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Surely I will sit in wait for them on Your straight path⁠﴾.

﴿beneath which rivers flow⁠﴾ is a qualifier of "ghurafan." ﴿Abiding therein⁠﴾ i.e., in the chambers, or in Paradise.

﴿How excellent is the reward of those who act⁠﴾ i.e., the righteous deeds. The object of praise is omitted, being confidently understood from what precedes it, and it is recited as (faniʿma).

"Those who are patient" (alladhina sabaru) may be an attributive adjective of "those who do [good deeds]" (al-'amilin), or it may be in the accusative as a term of praise (nusiba 'ala al-madh), meaning: they were patient under the harm of the polytheists, the hardships of emigration (al-muhajara), and other trials and difficulties.

"And upon their Lord they rely" (wa 'ala rabbihim yatawakkalun): that is, in what they undertake and what they leave undone, they rely upon none but God Most High.

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 29, verse 60:

﴿And how many a creature there is that does not carry its provision; Allah provides for it and for you.﴾ It is related that when the Prophet (ﷺ) commanded the believers who were in Makkah to emigrate to al-Madinah, they said: "How can we go to a town in which we have no livelihood?" So this verse was revealed. That is: and how many a creature there is that is unable to carry its provision, either because of its weakness, or because it does not store it, and it rises in the morning with no livelihood in its possession.

﴿Allah provides for it and for you.﴾ Then, despite its weakness and its reliance (on Allah), and despite your strength and your striving, it is equal in that He does not provide for it, or for you, except Allah the Exalted; for the provision of all, through means, is caused solely by Him. So do not fear poverty through emigration.

﴿And He is the All-Hearing﴾, the one who intensifies in hearing, so He hears this your statement.

﴿the All-Knowing﴾, the one who intensifies in knowledge, so He knows your inner thoughts.

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 29, verse 61:

﴿And if you were to ask them﴾ — that is, the people of Makkah.

﴿Who created the heavens and the earth and subjected the sun and the moon [to His service]? They will surely say, "Allah."﴾ — since there is no way for them to deny it, nor to hesitate about it.

﴿Then how are they turned away?﴾ — this is a rebuke and an expression of astonishment from Him, the Exalted, at their abandonment of acting in accordance with what this necessitates. That is: how are they turned away from acknowledging His sole divinity, while they acknowledge His sole [agency] in what He has mentioned of creation and subjugation?

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 29, verse 62:

﴿Allah extends provision to whomever He wills⦆ — that is, to extend it for him.

﴿of His servants, and restricts it for him⦆ — that is, He restricts it for whomever among them He wills to restrict it for, whoever he may be. Or the pronoun is indefinite, according to the indefiniteness of its referent; or it means He restricts it for whoever He extends it for in turn (ʿalā al-taʿāqub, i.e. alternately).

﴿Indeed Allah is All-Knowing of everything⦆ — so He knows who is suited to the extension of provision, and so extends it for him, and who is suited to its restriction, and so restricts it for him. Or: He knows that each of extension and restriction, at whatever time, accords with wisdom and benefit, so He does each of them at its time.

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 29, verse 63:

﴿And if you were to ask them, "Who sends down water from the sky and with it gives life to the earth after its death?" they would surely say, "Allah."﴾ Acknowledging that He is the One who brings into existence all contingent beings, both their roots and their branches, in their entirety. Then, they associate with Him some of His creatures, one that can hardly be imagined to have power over anything at all.

﴿Say: "Praise be to Allah."﴾ For having made the truth such that the wrongdoers do not dare to deny it, and that He has made clear Your proof against them. It was also said: for having preserved you from the likes of these misguided beliefs, though this interpretation is far-fetched. "But most of them do not know." That is, nothing of things, and therefore they do not know in accordance with the implication of this their statement, so they associate with Him, glorified is He, the most base of His creatures. It was also said: they do not understand what you intend by your praising Allah at their saying that.

(p-47) ﴿And this worldly life is nothing but amusement and play.﴾ This is an indication of contempt and belittlement of the world. And how could it not be, when the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "If the world were worth the wing of a mosquito in the sight of Allah, He would not have given a disbeliever a single drink of water from it." ﴿Nothing but amusement and play﴾ means: only as children are diverted and play with something, gathering around it and rejoicing in it for a while, then dispersing from it.

﴿And indeed, the Last Abode—that is the true life, if they only knew.﴾ That is: it is truly the abode of real life, because death and annihilation cannot befall it; or it is itself life, for emphasis. "Al-hayawan" is a verbal noun of "hayya" (to be alive), used to denote one who possesses life. Its original form is "hayayan," and the second yā' was changed to wāw because the pattern fa'alān carries the meaning of movement and agitation inherent in living creatures. For this reason it was preferred over "al-hayah" (life) in this context, which calls for emphasis.

﴿If only they knew﴾ means: they would not have preferred over it the world, whose origin is the absence of life, and whatever life arises in it is a fleeting accident, quick to vanish and swift to dissolve.

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 29, verse 65:

﴿So when they board the ship﴾ is connected to what is indicated by the description of their state. Rukub (riding, boarding) is ista'la' (being raised up) upon a moving thing, and it is transitive by itself, as in His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And horses, mules and donkeys, that you may ride them﴾. Its use here, and in similar cases, with the word "fi" (in) is to indicate that the thing ridden is in itself of the kind of places, and its movement is compulsory, not voluntary, as has passed in Surat Hud. The meaning is that they, in the state they were described as having (of associating partners with God), when they board the sea and are struck by hardship, ﴿they call upon God, sincerely devoted to Him in religion﴾, i.e., being in the form of those who are sincere in their religion among the believers, in that they call upon none other than God, exalted is He, knowing that none removes their calamities except Him.

﴿But when He delivers them safely to the land, behold, they associate partners [with Him]﴾, i.e., they immediately returned to associating partners.

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 29, verse 66:

﴿So that they may deny what We have given them, and so that they may enjoy themselves.﴾ That is: they suddenly return to associating partners [with God] so that they may become disbelievers in what We have given them of the blessing of deliverance, which it was their duty to be grateful for.

﴿But they will come to know﴾ That is: the outcome of that and its evil consequence, when they see the punishment.

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 29, verse 67:

﴿Have they not seen﴾ i.e., have they not looked and not witnessed?

﴿That We have made﴾ i.e., their land.

﴿A sanctuary secure﴾, protected from plunder and aggression, its people safe from every evil.

﴿While people are being snatched away from around them﴾ i.e., while they are being seized from around them by killing and captivity, since the Arabs around it were in constant raiding and plundering.

﴿Do they then believe in falsehood﴾ i.e., after the manifestation of the truth about which there is no doubt, do they believe specifically in falsehood, to the exclusion of the truth?!

﴿And in the favor of Allah do they disbelieve﴾, which is the one deserving of gratitude, by associating others with Him. And the placing of the relative clause (al-silah) first in both places (i.e., bi-al-batil and bi-ni'mat Allah) serves to show the complete heinousness of what they did.

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 29, verse 68:

﴿And who is more unjust than one who invents a lie against Allah,﴾ by claiming that He has a partner. That is, he is more unjust than every wrongdoer. Although the construction of the discourse indicates the negation of "more unjust" without explicitly negating the lesser evils, this has been mentioned repeatedly.

﴿Or denies the truth when it has come to him?﴾ That is, the Messenger or the Qur'an. In "lamma" (when) there is a rebuke against them, in that they did not hesitate and did not reflect when it came to them, but rather hastened to denial with the greatest haste (ātharu dhī athīr, lit. "the most eager of the eager," an idiom for rushing headlong).

﴿Is there not in Hell a dwelling for the disbelievers?﴾ This is an affirmation of their abiding therein, like the saying of the one who said:

"Are you not the best of those who rode the mounts?"

That is: do they not deserve to abide therein, since they have done what they have done of inventing lies against Allah the Exalted and denying the plain truth? Or it is a denial and an expression of astonishment at their audacity in regard to what has been mentioned of inventing lies and denial, despite their knowledge of the state of the disbelievers. That is: did they not know that in Hell there is a dwelling for the disbelievers, so that they dared this audacity?

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on Surah 29, verse 69:

﴿And those who strive in Us﴾, i.e., concerning Our affair. And [who strive] sincerely for Our sake. He used the word "striving" (mujahadah) without restriction so that it would encompass the struggle against both the outward and the inward enemies.

﴿We will surely guide them to Our paths﴾: the paths of journeying toward Us and of arriving at Our presence. Or [it means]: We will increase them in guidance to the paths of good and grant them success in following them, like His saying, ﴿And those who are guided, He increases them in guidance﴾. And in a hadith: "Whoever acts on what he knows, Allah will bequeath to him the knowledge of what he did not know." ﴿And indeed Allah is with the doers of good﴾: the being-with of help and support.

From him (ﷺ): "Whoever recites Surah al-'Ankabut will have ten good deeds recorded for him, equal to the number of every believer and hypocrite."
